rows.text: Benzene's physical profile — colourless liquid, bp 80.5 °C, mp 5.5 °C, density 0.879, water-immiscible, non-polar solvent, sooty flame — is one structure read by five instruments: flat symmetric disks pack (high mp), present broad faces (bp), refuse the water network (immiscibility), dissolve the non-polar (solvent list), and burn carbon-rich (flame).…

rows.text: ***The hexane comparison*** - n-hexane (86 g/mol) melts at -95 C while benzene (78 g/mol) melts at +5.5 C: shape, not mass, decides crystal packing.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Benzene's Physical Profile Benzene is a **colourless, mobile liquid** with a characteristic odour: bp 80.5 °C (80.1 °C in some texts), mp 5.5 °C, density 0.879 g/cm³ (lighter than water), immiscible with water, and an excellent solvent for non-polar and moderately polar solutes. Every one of these numbers has a structural reason.  ·  ## 2. Theorem Mirror - **State and appearance:** colourless liquid; characteristic (aromatic) odour; volatile. - **Boiling point 80.5 °C:** higher than cyclohexane (81 °C is close) but the comparison that matters — vs expected for its molar mass, benzene's planar disk shape gives strong instantaneous dipole dispersion contact.…

rows.text: ## 3. Deep Conceptual — Symmetry Packs, Shape Boils - **Melting point is a packing story:** 5.5 °C is high for a 78 g/mol molecule (cyclohexane, 84 g/mol, melts at 6.5 °C — similar, but n-hexane, 86 g/mol, melts at −95 °C!). rows.text: ## 5. Worked Example Types - **Type A — recite with reasons:** state each property with its structural cause. - **Type B — compare:** benzene vs cyclohexane vs hexane on mp/bp — the shape argument. - **Type C — miscibility prediction:** which of two solvents mixes with benzene, why.…  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **"Benzene is denser than water because it is aromatic":** 0.879 < 1 — it floats; aromaticity does not imply density. **"High mp means strong hydrogen bonding":** benzene has none — its mp is pure packing efficiency.
